question:
Eight \(1 \times 1\) square tiles are arranged as shown so their outside edges form a polygon with a perimeter of \(14\) units. Two additional tiles of the same size are added to the figure so that at least one side of each added tile is shared with a side of one of the squares in the original figure. Which of the following could be the perimeter of the new figure?

[Figure 1](figures/1992_AMC_8_Q22_question_fig1.svg)
solution:
The useful observation is that a shared side lies inside the figure and contributes nothing to its perimeter.

Add the tiles one at a time. Suppose an added tile shares \(k\) sides with the figure already present. Its attachment removes those \(k\) sides from the old boundary and contributes its other \(4-k\) sides. The perimeter therefore changes by
\[
(4-k)-k=4-2k.
\]
Each new tile must share a side with an original tile, so \(k\geq1\), even when adding the second tile. Consequently, each addition increases the perimeter by at most \(2\), and its change is always even. Starting from \(14\), the final perimeter must be even and cannot exceed
\[
14+2+2=18.
\]
This rules out the odd choices \(15,17,19\), as well as \(20\).

We must also show that \(18\) is possible. In the displayed figure, place one tile immediately to the left of the lower row and the other immediately to the right of the upper row. Each shares exactly one side with the original figure, and they do not share a side with each other. Each therefore adds \(2\) to the perimeter.

The resulting perimeter is \(\boxed{18}\) units, choice \(\boxed{\text{C}}\).

edges.reason: Written columns support perimeter arithmetic with larger dimensions. Adding decomposed lengths mentally gives the same result even for two-digit sides, so Gemini's chosen calculation does not establish column-method necessity.
The perimeter formulas use rectangle opposite-side equality and square side equality to combine their boundary lengths.
The explicit even-number units-digit criterion is the multiple-of-two units-digit test. The multiple-of-five part of the endpoint is outside this required scope.
edges.scope: stating the units-digit feature of even numbers

edges.reason: Uniform contributions are often totaled by multiplication, which helps. Double counting itself only needs two summations of one set, and either summation can be done by direct addition.
edges.scope: product counts of uniform incidence contributions
